records.title: Tŷ Mawr / Great House: the house and barn beside St Dochdwy’s churchyard, 29 July 1988 (recreation)
records.event: The Cadw inspection visit, when the farmhouse and barn photographs were taken
records.place_text: Tŷ Mawr / Great House, Llandough-juxta-Penarth, beside St Dochdwy’s churchyard
records.description:
The scene is the house and barn at Tŷ Mawr / Great House, Llandough, on 29 July 1988, the day of the Cadw inspection. Cadw’s two photographs of that day, a farmhouse photograph and a barn photograph, “both dated 29 July 1988” EV-0096; the farmhouse photograph is “Cadw farmhouse survey photograph, 29 July 1988” EV-0095 and the barn photograph “Cadw barn survey photograph, 1988” EV-0094.

The setting and materials: “Great House farmhouse and barn formed an attractive group, built of local lias limestone, and occupied an historic site next to the parish church” EV-0629. The house was “situated on edge of steep scarp, north of Llandough churchyard” EV-0630.

The exterior: “The external appearance i.e. the rendering, brick window surrounds, low pitched slate roof, and symmetrical front, immediately suggested a 19th century date” EV-0630; “Externally both farmhouse and barn appeared to be of nineteenth-century date” EV-0629. The older portion was “extensively 'modernized' in the 19th century by raising of roof eaves, replacement of window surrounds etc.” EV-0630.

The plan behind the front: “In plan the house consists of three rooms on the ground floor (aligned E–W)” EV-0630; “On the north side of the house, a wing had been added, probably in the 18th or early 19th century” EV-0630; “On the east side of the house further extensions had been made in the 19th century” EV-0630. The church beside it: “St Dochdwy's church dates from 1866” EV-0645.

Details taken from the barn photograph: grey rubble walls, slate roof, narrow ventilation slits, tall boarded doors and ivy.

Weather, planting and the yard surface on that day are not recorded beyond what the two photographs show.

Subject: an old two-storey Welsh farmhouse of local grey lias limestone rubble under old, flaking white limewash, with patches of bare grey stone showing through, especially on the unwashed right-hand gable. A long, low-pitched roof of grey Welsh slate with a line of red clay ridge tiles. Three chimney stacks: a rough stone stack on the left gable, a stone stack on the ridge left of centre, and a red-brick stack on the right gable. Background: behind the house, on slightly higher ground, mature trees and the stone west tower of a Victorian Welsh parish church with a steep gabled saddleback roof topped by a small cross, above a churchyard wall. records.title: Tŷ Mawr / Great House: the kitchen with its ogee-stopped beams, 26 April 1974 (recreation)
records.event: The RCAHMW ground-floor survey by H. J. Thomas
records.place_text: Tŷ Mawr / Great House, Llandough-juxta-Penarth, beside St Dochdwy’s churchyard
records.description:
The scene is the kitchen of Tŷ Mawr / Great House, Llandough, on 26 April 1974, the day H. J. Thomas of the Royal Commission recorded the ground floor (“Visited 26 April 1974. H.J. Thomas.” EV-0630; “H.J. Thomas, 26 April 1974 & 12 December 1988.” EV-0631).

The room: “on the east side a kitchen 16ft. 1ins. x 15ft. 6ins. having large fireplace (recently rebuilt on old lines) in east wall” EV-0630.

The beams: “Three beams survive, these being fairly massive about 11ins square (the upper part and joists concealed by plaster ceiling), adze cut, with plain broad chamfer and ogee stops” EV-0630. The measured plan keys the kitchen beams as “A Beams narrow chamfered. Ogee stops with torus.” EV-0631 and “C Beam narrow chamfered, ogee stops.” EV-0631; the 1988 description records “ogee-stopped beams” EV-0629 and, from the rubble, “an ogee-stopped beam with torus, a form of decoration that is not particularly common in Glamorgan” EV-0629.

The house around it: “To the west another chamber, probably the hall, separated by a passage 5ft. x 15ft. 3ins.” EV-0630; “The general plan, plus the fairly thick walls and the broad chamfered beams, suggest a 17th century date” EV-0630. Condition on the day: “much modernized” EV-0630. The ground floor “was surveyed in unusual circumstances in 1974” EV-0629; “Much detail was then concealed” EV-0629. A press report ten days earlier describes “magnificent oak beams” EV-0048.

made.prompt: A plain documentary interior photograph on 35 mm colour film, taken in flat grey daylight on 26 April 1974 for an architectural record, inside the kitchen of a seventeenth-century Glamorgan stone farmhouse. The room is about 16 feet by 15 feet with thick rubble-stone walls under old, slightly grubby whitewash and one deep-set small window. The subject is the ceiling: three massive dark oak beams, each about 11 inches square, spanning the room from side to side, roughly adze-cut with shallow, even tool marks only; the beam faces carry no carvings, no initials, no inscriptions and no graffiti of any kind. The lower edges of every beam are cut back in a plain broad chamfer, a clear flat bevel about two inches wide running along the beam, and near each wall the chamfer ends in a carved ogee stop, an S-curved step back to the square arris, clearly visible on the nearest beam. Between the beams a flat white plaster ceiling conceals the upper part of the beams and the joists. On the far (east) wall, a large open fireplace recently rebuilt on the old lines in rough local grey limestone, with a heavy timber lintel and a deep, empty hearth. Worn stone flag floor. Furniture kept minimal and ordinary for a working farmhouse in 1974: a plain scrubbed wooden table and two chairs; nothing styled, no flowers, no fruit, no decorative props. A plank door on the left leads to a narrow passage. No people. Camera: 24 mm lens at chest height from the west end of the room looking east, the three beams leading to the fireplace, the nearest beam's chamfer and ogee stop in sharp focus. Natural colour, true-to-life photographic texture, real lens and film grain, no CGI gloss, no over-processing, no HDR. records.title: Marconi and Kemp call at Great House, close on midnight, 10–11 May 1897 (recreation)
records.event: Marconi and George Kemp borrow the horse and trap to carry the apparatus to Lavernock Point
records.place_text: Tŷ Mawr / Great House, Llandough-juxta-Penarth, beside St Dochdwy’s churchyard
records.description:
The scene is the door of Great House, Llandough, close on midnight on the night of 10–11 May 1897, the eve of the Lavernock Point experiment.

The call: “The first happened at old Great House Farm in Llandough on the eve of May 11. Marconi was worried about the next day's experiment and had made some adjustment to the transmitter.” EV-0646 “It was a question of transporting the apparatus down to Lavernock Point late at night. Kemp was known to Farmer Williams, and thought perhaps they could borrow his horse and trap.” EV-0646

The door: “It was close on midnight when the two men called at the farm” EV-0646; “The men had to knock hard and it was some time before the bolts on the door were lifted.” EV-0646 “The door creaked open to reveal the farmer in night-cap and night-shirt carrying a blunderbuss, with members of his family grouped behind him.” EV-0646 “All went well, however, when Kemp produced a sovereign with which to hire the farmer's transport.” EV-0646

The stay and the work: “Marconi too slept here in a four poster bed whilst working with his experiments in wireless telegraphy between the Flat Holm and Lavernock Point.” EV-0645 The same entry is catalogued as “Glamorgan Village Book: printed page on Great House Farm demolition” EV-0085. At Lavernock, “Mr. Williams (of the engineering department, Cardiff) fixed upon Lavernock Point a pole 120 feet high, with a zinc cylinder at the summit” EV-0248; the trials were reported as “Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock” EV-0011.

The published sources differ on whether the first success came on 11 or 13 May 1897; the 1995 account places this call on the eve of 11 May, and that is the night shown.

made.prompt: A realistic documentary-style night photograph reconstructing a scene close on midnight on 10 May 1897 at an old farmhouse at Llandough near Cardiff, South Wales. Camera in the dark farmyard, slightly to one side of the door, so the farmer's face is clearly seen. The heavy plank front door of a two-storey farmhouse of white-limewashed rubble stone has just been unbolted and swung open, under a small gabled slate porch, worn stone step. In the doorway stands a stocky middle-aged Welsh farmer of about fifty: a fair-skinned, ruddy, weathered white European face with pale pink cheeks, grey-flecked brown side whiskers, sleepy wary expression. He wears a plain white cotton night-cap and a long plain white linen night-shirt to his shins, bare feet in old boots. In his left hand, raised near his chest, he holds a single lit tallow candle in a simple brass chamberstick; its warm golden light falls directly on his face, chest and both hands, so his features and pale skin are fully and clearly lit from the front. In his right hand an old brass-mounted blunderbuss hangs loosely at his side, muzzle pointing straight down at the stone step, not raised, not aimed. Behind him in the dim lamplit passage, family members in plain night clothes, faces soft and indistinct. Outside on the step, in three-quarter back view so their faces are not visible, two men in dark 1890s overcoats and bowler hats: the taller, slimmer young man holds a polished wooden box of telegraph apparatus with brass terminals under his arm; the older, stockier man holds out a small gold sovereign coin. To the right in the dark yard, a bay horse beside a two-wheeled Victorian trap, a hand lantern on the cobbles making a small pool of light. Deep blue night sky with faint stars, no moon. Warm candlelight on the farmer, cool night tones elsewhere. Natural colour, true-to-life photographic texture, real lens and film grain, no CGI gloss, no over-processing, no HDR, no staged props. The scene is the house site at Llandough on the morning of 6 December 1988, after the demolition.

The demolition: “The house and farm buildings were suddenly and completely demolished by B.P. A photograph of the aftermath is catalogued as “Photograph: Great House Farm ruins with the church” EV-0084.

The date on another record: the measured plan card carries the line “House demolished Nov. 1988.” EV-0631 Both dates are shown as recorded.
